readers.summary: The GPU model path is short. The scheduler thread (hls_gpu_scheduler.py:1297) gathers pinned-CPU avatar latents [B,8,32,32] (masked plus reference) and audio prompts [B,50,384], which already carry the sinusoidal positional encoding added on the CPU at job creation. It copies them to the GPU on the default stream and calls one static-batch-8 FP16 TensorRT engine. [measured-now: archive inspection] That engine is a single `_run_on_acc_0` TRT engine inside a TorchScript GraphModule (dynamo IR, C++ runtime, require_full_compilation, optimization_level default, num_avg_timing_iters=1, FP16 only). Timesteps are baked in as a constant 0 and no CUDA graphs are used. The scheduler then runs a torch.compile'd TAESD decoder (max-autotune, so inductor cudagraph trees, compiled per batch size) that emits the full 256x256 frame, followed by a GPU uint8 BGR pack and a blocking D2H. The scheduler also calls torch.cuda.synchronize after H2D, after the UNet and after the VAE by default (HLS_GPU_STAGE_SYNC_TIMING=1 and MUSETALK_VAE_DECODE_TIMING_SYNC=1; neither is overridden in the live server env [measured-now]). The UNet costs 177.8 GFLOP per frame [measured-now: FlopCounter on meta, matched analytically]: 3x3 convs 56%, GEGLU FF 22%, attention/projection GEMMs 14%, attention bmm 4.6%. By resolution the FLOPs are 36% at 32², 31% at 16², 27% at 8² and 5.5% at 4², but 84% of the 850M parameters sit in the 8²/4² stages. The measured 24.4-25.9 ms bs8 engine [doc] therefore achieves 55-58 TFLOPS, about 39% of the 142 TFLOPS FP16-accumulate peak, which is 2.4x above the ~1.25-1.35 ms/frame FP16 math floor. The whole model path costs 3.88-3.92 GPU-ms/frame (UNet ~3.05 + TAESD ~0.86) [doc: chin harness], a ~255 fps GPU ceiling that the pipelined harness already reaches at 250.8 fps. Reaching 300 fps needs <=3.33 ms/frame (-15%), realistically ~3.0 ms for live-path losses; 400 fps needs <=2.5 ms (-36%). The exact, low-risk levers stack to about 3.15-3.3 ms/frame (~305-317 fps ceiling), which is 300 with no margin: a native bs16 engine (-13% UNet, doc from the 3090), an exact TAESD row-crop (-35% TAESD FLOPs, bit-exact [measured-now]), removing stage syncs/pipelining, and TAESD TRT. So 300 delivered realistically also needs an INT8 W8A8 UNet. On GeForce Ada INT8 runs at 284 TOPS, while FP8 with FP32 accumulate runs at ~142, the same as FP16 with FP16 accumulate, so FP8 is not the math lever here, contrary to the 09-22 doc's ranking. With INT8 the projection is ~2.25-2.65 ms/frame (~375-445 fps). 400 fps with margin additionally needs block pruning plus distillation, or a win from verifying MHA fusion. Caching compute that depends only on the avatar frame is worth only 3.3% of UNet FLOPs, because audio cross-attention enters at the first transformer. DeepCache-style reuse does not apply to this single-step model. The binding practical constraints are 2.6 GB of free disk against a 2.21 GB engine per build, 12 GB of VRAM shared with a live server holding ~5 GB, and the pinned TRT 10.3 / torch_tensorrt 2.5 stack.

levers.name: Native static bs16 FP16 TRT UNet engine
levers.description: Build and validate an exact batch-16 engine to replace split-8, and load only that engine. Set HLS_SCHEDULER_MAX_BATCH=16 and FIXED_BATCH_SIZES=16, and warm TAESD at bs16 (MUSETALK_TAESD_WARMUP_BATCHES=16) so inductor does not compile on the live path.
levers.expected_gain: -12 to -14% UNet time: ~3.1 -> ~2.7 ms/frame, about +30-35 fps model-path ceiling
levers.evidence: [doc: docs/webrtc_generation_optimization_results_2026-07-03.md] On the 3090 the bs16 engine took 44.89 ms vs 2x25.86 ms (-13.2%) and passed validation. [doc: current_unet_trt_throughput_findings_2026-05-29.md] An earlier bs16 artifact FAILED validation (mae 0.018, max_abs 1.76). [doc: unet_probe.json] PyTorch 5.07 -> 4.44 ms/frame from bs8 to bs16. [inferred] At bs8 the 4x4 stage has arithmetic intensity 128 FLOP/B, below the 282 ridge, so it is weight-bound; weight streaming of 3.37 ms/batch halves per frame. Never built on this host.

levers.name: INT8 W8A8 UNet (ModelOpt SmoothQuant/per-channel, TRT Q/DQ)
levers.description: Quantize the conv and linear layers to INT8 and keep norms, softmax and fused MHA in FP16. Calibrate on real captured UNet I/O (the MUSETALK_UNET_CALIBRATION_CAPTURE path exists). Build through torch_tensorrt dynamo with ModelOpt fake-quant to avoid writing a 1.7-3.4 GB ONNX. Gate with capture mae/max_abs, SyncNet and a labelled video.
levers.evidence: [inferred] On GeForce Ada, INT8 dense is 284 TOPS vs FP16 142 (FP16-accumulate) / 71 (FP32-accumulate). The engine currently runs at ~39% of the FP16-acc peak (55.8 TFLOPS = 8 x 177.8 GF / 25.5 ms). Weights 1.70 -> 0.85 GB. A single-step model means no error compounding across denoising steps. Caution [doc: SoulX PRO_40FPS_ITERATION_LOG]: on this same GPU, INT8 was at parity for Conv3d. The Conv2d/GEMM IMMA kernels are mature, but this must be measured. UNet quantization has never been attempted in MuseTalk (all INT8 history is VAE-only).

levers.name: FP8 E4M3 UNet
levers.description: ModelOpt FP8_DEFAULT_CFG with a TRT FP8 build (settable on TRT 10.3).
levers.expected_gain: 1.0-1.15x on this GeForce card: gains come only from halved weight and activation bytes
levers.evidence: [inferred: Ada GeForce spec] FP8 with FP32 accumulate is ~142 TFLOPS, equal to FP16 with FP16 accumulate, so it is not a math lever unless the engine is on FP32-acc kernels. [doc: SoulX log] TRT 10.9 on this GPU had no FP8 Conv3d kernel; FP8 Conv2d support in TRT 10.3 on sm_89 is unverified. The 09-22 doc ranked FP8 first; INT8 should outrank it.

levers.name: Verify/force fused attention for 32x32 self-attention (head_dim 40)
levers.description: Inspect the engine (IEngineInspector/nsys) for MHA fusion at 32² (1024 tokens, 8 heads x 40). If unfused, fix via a TRT upgrade, a plugin, or an attention-only restructure.
levers.expected_gain: 0-20% of UNet time. If unfused, the score tensor [8,8,1024,1024] fp16 = 134 MB means ~0.5 GB of DRAM traffic per layer (~1.07 ms) x 5 layers, about 5.3 ms of each 25.5 ms batch
levers.evidence: [measured-now] heads=8, head_dim 40/80/160, AttnProcessor2_0; self-attn bmm is 6.71 GF/frame at 32² vs 0.84 at 16². [inferred] Traffic arithmetic. Fusion status is unknown without GPU inspection.

levers.description: Use optimization_level 5, num_avg_timing_iters >1 and max_aux_streams, reuse the timing cache, and check the accumulation precision of the chosen tactics.
levers.expected_gain: 0-5% UNet
levers.evidence: [measured-now: compile settings pickled in unet_trt.ts] enabled_precisions={f16}, optimization_level=None (default 3), num_avg_timing_iters=1, workspace 2 GiB, sparse_weights False, max_aux_streams None.

levers.description: Newer Myelin fusions, MHA kernels and INT8/FP8 conv kernels for sm_89. The SoulX venv on this machine already runs TRT 10.9 with torch 2.7.1.
levers.expected_gain: 0-10% FP16; likely needed to get the best INT8/FP8 result
levers.evidence: [doc: SoulX log header: torch 2.7.1+cu128, TRT 10.9.0.34 on this GPU]. [measured-now] The MuseTalk venv is pinned to torch 2.5.1, torch_tensorrt 2.5.0 and TRT 10.3.

levers.name: Exact TAESD row-crop with stage-wise halo
levers.description: TAESD has no normalization layers, so cropping each stage's input to the rows its outputs need is exact. Required input start rows per layer for r0=104: [0,0,0,0,1,4,9,10,13,16,19,39,40,43,46,49,99,100,103,104]. The latent stage must stay full height, because output row 104 depends on latent row 0. The decoder returns rows r0..256; compose then pastes them into a 256 buffer or its plan is offset.
levers.expected_gain: TAESD FLOPs 35.3 -> 23.1 GF/frame (65.4%) at r0=104: ~0.86 -> ~0.55-0.65 ms/frame, about +5-8% total fps
levers.evidence: [measured-now: CPU FP32 with real TAESD weights] max|diff| vs full decode = 0.0 at r0=104/110/128. [doc: roi_waste.json] Blended rows start at 110/111 (latent-aligned 104) on the measured avatars. r0 must be per-avatar and must cover the chin-alignment warp support.

levers.name: TAESD engine-level speedups (TRT FP16 / INT8, channels_last, fused uint8 pack)
levers.description: TAESD achieves only ~41 TFLOPS-equivalent (29% of FP16-acc peak). It is DRAM-bound at 256² (8x64x256x256 fp16 = 67 MB per activation). Candidates: build it in TRT, fold the /2+0.5, clamp, x255 and BGR pack into the graph, and try channels_last, which should help here because TAESD has no GroupNorm.
levers.expected_gain: -0.1 to -0.25 ms/frame on top of the crop
levers.evidence: [measured-now] 35.34 GFLOP/frame, 55% at 256². [doc: taesd.json] eager 12.3 ms -> compiled 6.82 ms (launch-bound). [inferred] The INT8 variant would carry medium risk.

levers.name: Remove per-stage syncs and pipeline GPU batches in the live scheduler
levers.description: Disable the timing syncs (HLS_GPU_STAGE_SYNC_TIMING=0, MUSETALK_VAE_DECODE_TIMING_SYNC=0; one-line rollback). Double-buffer the pinned staging and output buffers, put D2H on a side stream with events, and assemble batch N+1 while batch N runs.
levers.expected_gain: No change to GPU ms, but moves the live server from serial-like behavior toward the GPU-bound ceiling (offline: +17-23%)
levers.evidence: [doc: experiments/chin_fps_validation_20260927] Serial 204.6-215 fps vs pipelined 250.8 fps at identical 3.88-3.92 GPU-ms/frame, with bit-identical output hashes. [measured-now: /proc/3240171/environ] The live server does not override the sync flags, whose defaults are on (hls_gpu_scheduler.py:230, vae.py:30).

levers.name: CUDA graphs / direct TRT runtime for the UNet
levers.description: Call torch_tensorrt.runtime.set_cudagraphs_mode(True), which the C++ runtime supports but the repo never calls, or drive an IExecutionContext directly with pre-allocated I/O and explicit streams.
levers.expected_gain: 0-2% offline (a single 25 ms enqueue already runs ahead of the GPU); 1-4% under live CPU/GIL contention
levers.evidence: [measured-now] The archive holds exactly one TRT engine and no PyTorch fallback segments, so wrapper overhead is small. [inferred-from-code] torch_tensorrt 2.5 ships _cudagraphs.py. [doc: SoulX log] CUDA graphs were dead where the host already ran ahead of the GPU.

levers.name: Fused model step (UNet + cropped TAESD + uint8 pack as one graph/engine)
levers.description: Capture the whole per-batch GPU step in one CUDA graph, or put TAESD in the same TRT engine, so each batch has one launch and one D2H.
levers.expected_gain: -0.05 to -0.15 ms/frame (inter-stage bubbles), plus lower CPU load
levers.evidence: [inferred-from-code] Today there are three separately launched stages with syncs between them (hls_gpu_scheduler.py:1443-1472).

levers.name: UNet block pruning + distillation (BK-SDM style)
levers.description: Remove resnet+attention pairs where the FLOPs are, not where the parameters are. The 32²/16² stages hold 67% of FLOPs but 16% of params. Candidate cut: one pair from each of down_blocks.0/1/2 and up_blocks.1/2/3, plus the mid attention, about 58-61 GF (33-34%). Distill from the 850M teacher with feature KD plus SyncNet loss (train.py exists).
levers.expected_gain: 1.3-1.5x UNet (stacks with INT8); needed for 400 fps with margin
levers.evidence: [measured-now: per-unit table] Each 32² resnet+attention pair is ~9.4-11.7 GF; up_blocks.2/3 together are 43% of FLOPs. [doc: SoulX log] Block bypass plus decoder distillation shipped on this GPU. Training an 850M model on a 12 GB card needs 8-bit optimizers and checkpointing, or a cloud GPU.

levers.name: Source-only (avatar-frame-only) compute caching
levers.description: Cache, per unique cycle frame: conv_in + down_blocks.0.resnets.0 (before the first cross-attention), and the skip-channel half of up_blocks.3.resnets.2 conv1 and its shortcut. The latter is exact because the concat puts the skip channels in separate GroupNorm groups.
levers.expected_gain: <=3.3% of UNet FLOPs (5.9 GF/frame), about -0.08 ms/frame
levers.evidence: [measured-now analytic] conv_in 0.05 + resnet0 3.78 + skip halves ~2.1 GF. Needs an engine split and ~2 MB of VRAM per unique source frame (~600 MB for a 300-unique-frame avatar). Poor ROI.

levers.name: Cross-frame deep-feature reuse (DeepCache analog)
levers.description: Reuse the 8²/4² features from the previous frame. There is no cross-timestep reuse to exploit because MuseTalk is single-step with t=0 baked in.
levers.expected_gain: <=10-15% with every-other-frame reuse (the deep stages are 32% of FLOPs)
levers.evidence: [inferred-from-code] Audio enters through cross-attention in every transformer, including the 8² and mid 4² stages, so reuse stales the lip conditioning. timesteps is baked as a buffer (tensorrt_export.py:211).

levers.name: ROI-cropped UNet (retrained on the lower latent rows)
levers.description: Only latent rows ~13..32 of the UNet output are ever blended. A crop cannot be exact because attention and downsampling are global. A retrained model on 32x24 rows would cut ~25% of FLOPs.
levers.expected_gain: ~1.25x UNet
levers.evidence: [doc: roi_waste.json] Used rows 110..256 of 256. [inferred] Global attention at 32² mixes all rows.

levers.name: 2:4 structured sparsity (TRT sparse_weights, Ada sparse tensor cores)
levers.description: ASP-style 2:4 pruning plus a sparse fine-tune of the conv and GEMM weights.
levers.expected_gain: 1.1-1.3x UNet realistically (2x math only on eligible layers)
levers.evidence: [measured-now] Engine settings show sparse_weights=False. Requires training; stacks with INT8.

levers.name: Larger static batches (bs24/bs32)
levers.description: Static engines beyond bs16.
levers.expected_gain: +0-5% over bs16, at the cost of added latency and VRAM
levers.evidence: [doc: unet_probe.json] PyTorch 4.44 -> 4.375 -> 4.195 ms/frame at bs16/24/32. [inferred] Weight streaming already drops below 0.14 ms/frame by bs24.

levers.name: Multiple concurrent contexts/streams on one GPU
levers.description: Run two UNet contexts or sessions concurrently to fill idle SMs.
levers.evidence: [doc: SoulX PRO_40FPS log] Two sessions gave +1.3% aggregate on this same card. The MuseTalk UNet is already compute-bound and GPU-saturated.

constraints: Budget: 300 fps = 3.33 GPU-ms/frame all-in; 400 fps = 2.5 ms. The current model path is 3.88-3.92 ms/frame [doc: chin harness], so it must drop by 15% (300) or 36% (400) before any live-path losses.

UNet = 177.8 GFLOP/frame, 849.9M params [measured-now]. FP16 math floor is 1.25 ms/frame at 142 TFLOPS (FP16 accumulate) and 2.5 ms/frame at 71 TFLOPS (FP32 accumulate). INT8 floor is 0.63 ms/frame [inferred]. Measured is 3.05-3.24 ms/frame [doc].

GeForce Ada rates: FP32-accumulate tensor math runs at half rate. FP8 with FP32 accumulate (~142 TFLOPS) equals FP16 with FP16 accumulate, so only INT8 (284 TOPS) doubles the math ceiling [inferred: Ada spec].
Power limit is 220 W and equals the maximum limit, so it cannot be raised. SM clock can reach 3105 MHz. Memory is 21 Gbps x 192-bit = 504 GB/s, L2 is 48 MB [measured-now: nvidia-smi].

VRAM is 12 GB and the live server holds ~5 GB. Each UNet engine file is 2.21 GB. Co-loading bs8 and bs16 engines, or building while the live server runs, risks OOM: dual engines OOMed on a 24 GB 3090, and the INT8 VAE could not be co-resident with the TRT UNet on this card [doc].

Disk has 2.6 GB free (99% full). One engine is 2.21 GB, an FP16 UNet ONNX ~1.7 GB, an FP32 ONNX ~3.4 GB. Any rebuild needs freed space, e.g. models/trt_downloaded_backup_20260915 (2.2 GB), which is the user's decision, or another volume. This turn is read-only.

The engine has static shapes: batch_range [8,8], latent [B,8,32,32], encoder_hidden_states [B,50,384], FP16, timesteps baked to 0. The scheduler must pad to the engine batch, and MultiTrtUnetBackend only splits into exact multiples (trt_runtime.py:1594-1638).
Stack is pinned: torch 2.5.1+cu121, torch_tensorrt 2.5.0, TensorRT 10.3, ModelOpt 0.23.2, diffusers 0.30.2. An upgrade needs a separate venv.
TAESD is compiled per batch size (dynamic=False, vae_fast_decoder.py:143), so every new scheduler batch size must be warmed or it compiles on the live path.
TAESD takes the scaled UNet latent directly (no 1/0.18215 division) and returns [-1,1] -> /2+0.5 clamp. Output is always the full 256x256 frame in fp16.

All GPU work is issued from one scheduler thread on the default CUDA stream, with a synchronize after each stage by default. The torch_tensorrt C++ runtime may use a pool stream with event syncs internally [inferred].

Quality gates: UNet capture validation (meta max_mae 0.01, max_abs 0.5; current bs8 mae_max 0.0020). The user requires TAESD with 100% chin alignment. Standing memory requires a labelled comparison video for any lossy lever, with a one-line rollback.
Only the lower-face rows (~104/110..256 of the 256 decode) are blended, and the decode is then resized to the face bbox (~0.53 area ratio) [doc: roi_waste.json].
open_questions: Which kernels does the FP16 TRT UNet engine run: HMMA with FP16 accumulate or FP32 accumulate? And is the 32² head_dim-40 self-attention a fused MHA? This decides whether INT8 or FP8 is the lever and whether up to ~20% of UNet time is in unfused attention. It needs nsys or IEngineInspector on the GPU; the TRT mae 0.0014-0.002 vs PyTorch-compile 0.0003 hints at FP16 accumulation.
What is the sustained SM clock during a continuous UNet loop at the 220 W cap (is it power-throttling)? This sets the true peak (142 TFLOPS at 2.475 GHz, up to ~160 at ~2.8 GHz).
Why is the engine file 2.21 GB when the FP16 weights are 1.70 GB? Are some layers stored or executed in FP32?
Does a native bs16 engine pass the capture validation gate on this host with TRT 10.3? A 2026-05-29 bs16 artifact failed (mae 0.018, max_abs 1.76); the 2026-07-04 one passed on the 3090.

What does INT8 do to lip-sync and teeth quality? The UNet has never been quantized in this project. A SyncNet metric plus labelled video gate is needed, and the calibration corpus must come from real captures across several avatars.
What is the safe TAESD crop start row per avatar once the 100% chin-alignment warp and upper-neck support are included? Does the warp read decoded rows above 104?

How much of the model-path gain survives the live WebRTC path? Live capacity with TAESD has never been measured beyond 2-3 streams, and historically the live path plateaued near 112 fps on the RTX 6000 Ada.
Is training compute available for pruning plus distillation? An 850M-param teacher/student on a 12 GB card needs 8-bit optimizers and checkpointing, or cloud GPUs.
Can ~5 GB of disk be freed, or another volume mounted, for engine builds and optional ONNX/INT8 artifacts?

readers.summary:
Short answer: 300 fps can't be reached by fixing the serving path alone. But the serving path is what caps the server well below the GPU limit today, and that is fixable.

**How the server runs.** It is one uvicorn process with one asyncio event loop. That loop hosts every aiortc PeerConnection and does four jobs: paces recv(), decodes the idle mp4 for idle sessions, converts BGR frames to yuv420p inside push_bgr_frames_batch, and builds, encrypts and sends RTP. A single 'hls-gpu-scheduler' thread runs select → assemble → H2D → TRT UNet → compiled TAESD → .cpu().numpy(), with three torch.cuda.synchronize() calls per batch (HLS_GPU_STAGE_SYNC_TIMING defaults to on) [inferred-from-code]. Compose runs in a 10-thread pool, libx264 encode runs in aiortc's default executor, and everything shares one GIL [inferred-from-code].

**Overlap in the live path is only partial.** Compose for batch N does overlap GPU batch N+1. But the WebRTC handoff for batch N runs on the scheduler thread between GPU batches. That handoff is the pose crossfade copies plus frame_batch_callback, which blocks on run_coroutine_threadsafe(...).result() while the event loop converts 8 frames. Batch N+1 is also never queued before batch N's D2H has finished.
- Result: about 8–10 ms of GPU idle per 31.5 ms bs8 batch, so a single process tops out around 195–200 fps [inferred from doc wall_api.log: GPU batch 31.5 ms, callback ≈1 ms/frame].
- It gets worse under load. In my loopback test with half the sessions idle, the per-batch push handoff reached p50 75 ms [measured-now].

**Batching in the live env.** HLS_SCHEDULER_MAX_BATCH=8, buckets [8], static bs8 engine. The round-robin cursor gives one job 8 frames per turn. Padding happens only when fewer than 8 frames are available. There is no deadline awareness, and a full 400-frame strict-FIFO queue can block the scheduler thread for up to 30 s [inferred-from-code].

**Idle sessions use no GPU, but they still cost encode and transport.** Between turns there is no GPU work. However, exact_silence turns and WEBRTC_RAW_IDLE_POSE frames still run UNet+TAESD and then throw the output away [inferred-from-code]. So GPU demand equals speaking frames only, while encode and transport demand is every session × 20 fps.

**What the loopback aiortc harness showed (one sender process, one loop, 512x896, no GPU):**
- **Idle sessions with the current per-frame decode on the loop:** the loop saturates at about 180–186 fps total (98% busy, loop-lag p99 170–280 ms).
- **Live-pushed frames:** 300 and 400 fps with the loop at 46% and 62%.
- **Pre-decoded idle cache plus libx264 veryfast with one thread:** 15 and 20 mixed sessions at 300 and 400 fps, using 1.9 and 2.6 cores with the loop at 36% and 47% [measured-now].

**The NVENC patch never runs.** It is dead code on aiortc 1.14, because H264Encoder hardcodes libx264. The live log shows codec=libx264. That encoder costs 11.5–14.8 CPU-ms per frame and starts 28 threads per encoder [measured-now]. NVENC itself works through PyAV at 0.12 CPU-ms per frame, but this GeForce driver allows only 12 NVENC sessions [measured-now].

**Why the RTX 6000 Ada plateaued around 112 fps.** That plateau was model-bound: the SD-VAE INT8 decoder dominated, and aggregate fps matched batch / avg_gpu_batch [doc]. The serving overheads were hidden by the slow decoder. They are all still in today's code, and now that TAESD has cut GPU time per frame by about 4–5x, they matter.

**The user's live 10-stream run on the restarted server.** This was pid 3305906, around 19:35–19:39 UTC. Only about 120–128 of roughly 177 output frames per stream were fresh; 49–77 were held or duplicated. avg_gpu_batch was 36–40 ms, the callback max was 103–145 ms, process CPU was 5.4–8.9 cores and there were over 1000 threads. Ten idle sessions alone used 3.9–12.5 cores. The process died at 19:39:24 with no shutdown log line and 0.8 GB of RAM available, so it was probably OOM-killed [doc: wall_api.log RESOURCE lines].

aiortc 1.14 H264Encoder hardcodes libx264 in _encode_frame. Any encoder change must patch that method or override the codec registry, and the existing create_encoder_context patch is a no-op [inferred-from-code + doc log codec=libx264].
One asyncio loop per process owns all aiortc PeerConnections. The loop saturates (98%) at ≈180-186 fps total output when idle clips are decoded on it [measured-now].
Encode/transport load = all connected sessions x 20 fps, idle or speaking. GPU load = speaking frames only.
TAESD is torch.compile max-autotune, which uses CUDA-graph trees that are thread-affine. Keep every GPU launch (UNet, TAESD, whisper prep ideally on its own stream) on a consistent thread.
Whisper feature encode for each new turn runs on the same device and default stream from a prep thread, so it serializes with UNet batches [inferred-from-code].

VRAM is 12 GB and one server holds ≈5 GB, so at most 2 full replicas fit. RAM is 30 GB (cgroup max 31.1 GB, oom_kill=7 recorded). A BGR avatar cycle is 1.38 MB/frame (≈330 MB per 240-frame 512x896 clip) and a yuv cache adds 0.69 MB/frame. Distinct avatars x poses per server are RAM-bound.
Strict FIFO (400-frame queue, 30 s push timeout) plus the blocking callback lets one far-ahead session stall the shared scheduler thread [inferred-from-code].

Chin alignment (user-required) is offline-only. It needs FaceMesh in a separate venv (protobuf incompatibility), about 3 ms/frame of tracking, and a one-frame jaw lookahead, so a multi-process tracking pool is required for 300 fps (≈0.9 core).
Kokoro TTS runs in-process on CPU via asyncio.to_thread (KOKORO_TTS_DEVICE=cpu). At 15 streams it must move out of process or it competes for the GIL.

readers.summary: The chin path does not stop 300 fps, or even 400 fps. It costs zero extra GPU time: the same GPU work ran at 250.8 fps in the standard pipelined arm [doc: chin_fps_validation_20260927/taesd_pipelined_results.json]. On the CPU it costs about 7-8 core-ms per frame, against about 1.5-1.8 core-ms for the standard path [measured-now]. That is roughly 2.1-2.5 cores at 300 fps and 2.8-3.4 cores at 400 fps under light load. Under full-machine SMT and clock contention, budget about 1.4x: 3-3.6 cores at 300 fps and 4-4.8 at 400 fps [inferred]. That still fits a 16-core 7950X with more than 11 physical cores left for VP8, WebRTC and TTS. The documented chin rates (184.9/193.4 fps for chin100 v1, 168.8/163.4 for the accepted seam-v1, 148-171 across the six diversity avatars) are limits of a single-threaded offline harness, not of the machine. One Python thread did per-frame FaceMesh IPC (about 3.25 ms) and then refined compose (about 2.3-3.2 ms) in series, with only one GPU batch prefetched [doc]. The real ceiling is architectural. First, refined compose in threads plateaus at about 830 fps per process because of the GIL (about 1.2 ms of each ~3 ms frame is Python or small-numpy work). Run as processes it scales to 2046 fps with 8 and 2424 with 16 [measured-now]. Second, FaceMesh tracking mode is stateful and sequential per stream: one graph per stream, frames in order, which needs per-stream ordered actors instead of today's free 10-thread compose pool. Third, the accepted 3-tap jaw filter needs the next frame's delta. That holds the last frame of each per-stream chunk until the next chunk arrives, costing latency (at most one frame, 50 ms at 20 fps) but no throughput. FaceMesh on the CPU is the largest single exact cost: 2.98 ms wall and 1.07 cores per frame. It is deterministic (a fresh rerun reproduced the saved landmarks at 0.0 px) and scales across processes: 292 fps with 1 process, 626 with 2, 1633 with 8 [measured-now]. The chin path is not in the live server today. api_avatar.compose_frame applies only static per-cycle blend plans. Commit c284891 added static cheek, source-mouth and side-jaw mask variants behind env flags; none are set on the live server. There is no generated-face tracking or warp anywhere in api_server, the scheduler or api_avatar. The chinese_bob WebRTC README states the same. Exact CPU levers work: prototype numba nogil kernels matched production output bit for bit, cutting the fixed-point blend from 0.50 to 0.19 ms and the chin warp from 0.71-0.91 to 0.19 ms (0 mismatches over 720 frames, 3 identities) [measured-now]. Porting the mask the same way should bring refined compose from about 3 ms to about 1 ms [inferred]. After that, FaceMesh (about 3.3 core-ms) is about 60-75% of chin CPU. The cheap alternatives to it are all approximate at the 0.3-2.4 px level on the jaw and lip points, which is the same scale as the chin errors being corrected [measured-now]. A GPU landmark net would spend the one resource that actually binds at 300 fps (3.33 ms of GPU per frame), so tracking should stay on the CPU in worker processes. One more finding: NumPy 2 changes `lip_y` from float64 to float32 [measured-now]. This is a likely root cause of the cross-environment pixel differences the seam docs noticed but could not explain. Composition must stay in the TRT env's NumPy 1.23.5 / OpenCV 4.9, or be ported with explicit dtypes.

levers.description: Move per-stream tracking, the seam-v1 mask, blend, warp and optionally the YUV conversion out of the api_server process into worker processes. Use per-stream ordered actors (tracking state and lookahead need ordering), shared-memory rings for faces in and I420/BGR out, and avatar frames and chin caches in /dev/shm, mapped read-only. Put it behind one flag (e.g. MUSETALK_CHIN_ALIGN) for a one-line rollback.
levers.expected_gain: Removes about 1.2 ms/frame of server GIL time (36% of one GIL at 300 fps, 48% at 400). Chin post capacity goes from about 160-190 fps (serial harness) and about 830 fps (in-process threads) to more than 2000 fps aggregate. Server-side cost per frame becomes about 0.1-0.25 ms (shm bookkeeping + VideoFrame wrap).

Build the tracker input inside the tracker from shared source frames plus the already-resized face (resized once, in the TRT env).

That changes lip_y in the warp and is a likely cause of the unexplained cross-environment pixel drift [doc: chin_seam_refinement README]. Pixel parity must be re-proved with verify_baseline.py. Disk has only 2.6 GB free.

constraints: Chin compose must run in the TRT venv's NumPy 1.23.5 / OpenCV 4.9 (or a port with explicit dtypes). NumPy 2 (NEP 50) changes scalar promotion (lip_y float64 -> float32) and so changes raw pixels [measured-now]. FaceMesh needs mediapipe 0.10.9 in the SoulX venv (its protobuf conflicts with the TRT venv), so there is at least one process boundary today.

FaceMesh tracking mode is stateful: one graph per stream (about 31 MB RSS and 33 threads each [measured-now]), frames fed strictly in order, reset per turn, and the first frame costs about 14 ms for detection. Cross-stream batching is impossible with the stock graph.

The accepted symmetric 3-tap jaw filter needs the next frame's delta. Composition must be ordered per stream, and the last frame of each chunk waits for the next chunk (at most 1 frame, 50 ms at 20 fps). End of turn uses edge padding.

The current live compose pool (hls_gpu_scheduler.py:193-205: max(6, compose_workers, min(10, cpu//2)) = 10 threads) can run two batches of the same stream at once and reorders later. That is incompatible with the stateful tracker and the lookahead without per-stream actors.

GIL: in-process refined compose holds about 1.2 ms/frame (830 fps plateau). The PyAV bgr24 wrap holds about 0.38 ms/frame in the asyncio loop. The server's shared process also carries the GPU scheduler and aiortc.

Memory: the current chin caches take 8.5 MB per source frame (about 2 GB per 240-frame pose). RAM is 30 GB with 6-9 GB available during this run; /dev/shm is 15 GB with 6.2 GB free. Caches must be trimmed and shared.

Chin math is valid only on the prepared source frame whose landmarks p[i] were tracked. Motion-atlas decoded backgrounds, pose crossfades and current-phoneme raw/alpha layers need a policy: the warp changes pixels outside the returned alpha support.

Exactness gates available: verify_baseline.py (480 accepted Japanese/Latina frames, zero difference) and pixel_checks (protected lip change 0, warp Jacobian > .25). Cross-decoder or live audio has no bit-exact reference; live output needs visual review.
GPU is the binding resource at 300 fps (3.33 ms/frame budget versus about 3.9 ms/frame UNet+TAESD today), so CPU work should not move onto the GPU unless the CPU becomes binding.
Disk: about 2.6 GB free on the overlay, so there is no room for large new venvs or model exports without cleanup.
open_questions: Live per-frame CPU and GIL cost of VP8 encode plus aiortc RTP/SRTP/ICE at 15-20 concurrent streams was not measured here. It decides how much of the ~11 spare cores and of the event-loop GIL remain.

How far do per-frame costs inflate under real full-server load? FaceMesh fps per process fell from 292 (1 process) to 204 (8 processes) and 106 (16 processes) while other sessions were also using the CPU. The 1.4x contention factor used here is an estimate.
Is a numba port of RefinedMask.current also bit-exact (with np.rint, the distance/feather float32 promotion and the region/guard combine)? Blend and warp are proven; the mask is not yet written.

What should the live fallback be when FaceMesh loses the generated face (the harness raises RuntimeError), when the pose router switches source or background mid-chunk, or on barge-in? Options include standard compose for that frame or holding the previous delta; all need visual review.
Would a merged NumPy 1.23.5 / OpenCV 4.9 / mediapipe 0.10.9 venv keep FaceMesh landmarks and composite pixels identical to the current two-venv result?
What average chin load should we plan for? Idle and exact-silence frames skip generation and chin, so the conversational duty cycle could sit well below the 300-400 fps peak design point.

readers.summary: The audio side of MuseTalk is almost free on the GPU. Whisper, the per-turn setup work and local text-to-speech (TTS) do not stand in the way of 300 fps, as long as TTS never runs on this box. Each turn is one complete audio file uploaded to POST /webrtc/sessions/{id}/stream (there is no streamed-audio input). The server decodes that file 4-5 times: a PyAV exact-silence check, an ffmpeg decode to 16 kHz for edge-silence trimming, an optional ffmpeg trim, a probe, and an ffmpeg conversion to 48 kHz for RTP. Then hls_gpu_scheduler._prepare_job runs librosa.load (24->16 kHz), the HF WhisperFeatureExtractor (mel padded to 30 s) and whisper-tiny's encoder (8.2M params, 4 layers, d=384, fp16, on the GPU's default CUDA stream, prep thread). The encoder keeps all 5 hidden states, so each frame's prompt is 10 steps x 5 layers = [50,384]. Measured warm on CPU: librosa.load 1.2 ms and mel 1.4 ms per 7.3 s turn [measured-now]. Live logs show the whole prep_work (audio features + GPU Whisper encode + pose-plan compile) at 0.01-0.02 s per warm turn, for turns of 3-24 s [doc: /workspace/experiments/*/ logs, n>150 turns]. The documented '0.88 s for 8 s audio' matches the first-turn cold cost (0.60-0.86 s prep in logs). That cost is librosa's lazy first call (1.2 s cold [measured-now]), which _warm_runtime_paths does not warm; it is not the Whisper model. Whisper's cost is per turn, not per frame: the encoder always processes a 30 s window (~37 GFLOP [inferred-from-code]). At 300 fps with ~7 s turns that is about 2 turns/s, roughly 0.2-1% of the GPU budget (upper bound about 4%). So batching Whisper across streams, TRT/FP16 Whisper, or CPU Whisper cannot move the 300 fps needle. Moving it to CPU would cost 0.6-2.4 cores, because the CPU encoder takes 48-377 ms per window [measured-now], and CPU is the scarcer resource here. Shorter encoder windows and incremental (prefix) encoding change the features by 10-24% relative error [measured-now], and the encoder is bidirectional, so both are quality risks for no throughput gain. Kokoro-82M is an in-process test endpoint (KOKORO_TTS_DEVICE=cpu on the live server, a single RLock serializes calls); production TTS is designed as a separate Chatterbox pool (docs/chatterbox_autoscaling_plan.md). Measured Kokoro on CPU costs 0.62-1.82 thread-seconds per second of audio (RTF 0.114 at 16 threads, 0.22 at 4, 0.62 at 1) [measured-now]. That equals 31-91 thread-ms per generated frame against a CPU budget of ~107 thread-ms per frame at 300 fps, so local CPU TTS alone would take 30-85% of the machine. GPU Kokoro is inferred (not measured) at 15-45% of the 3.33 ms/frame GPU budget, so TTS must stay off-box. Idle frames cost no GPU: between turns the tracks play the idle/motion MP4 as raw frames, and scheduler jobs exist only during a turn. Idle sessions still cost CPU (roughly 0.5 core per idle session in logs: decode, libx264 at 30 fps playback, Opus silence at 5-9 ms per stream-second [measured-now]). No doc gives a speaking/idle duty cycle. Whole-turn audio plus a 400-frame run-ahead queue lets the GPU smooth bursts. With 300 fps of model capacity, a binomial estimate at 50% speaking duty gives about 20 connected calls at p99, and 15 calls need only 240 fps at p99. Two exact-output GPU wastes exist: exact-silence turns and WEBRTC_RAW_IDLE_POSE frames still run UNet+VAE and throw the output away (hls_gpu_scheduler.py:1770; the doc says it 'does not optimize away GPU inference'). Per-turn HTTP setup is p50 140 ms / p90 204 ms / p99 368 ms (uncontended logs), plus first block 0.24-0.36 s. That is latency, not throughput, but its ffmpeg/to_thread work shares the default asyncio executor with aiortc's per-packet audio/video encoders.

constraints: Whisper-tiny encoder input is fixed at 3000 mel frames (30 s): transformers 4.39 raises otherwise (modeling_whisper.py:1164), and MuseTalk was trained on 30 s-padded windows. Per-turn Whisper cost is constant for any turn up to 30 s.

Whisper's encoder is bidirectional, so features depend on later audio in the window; exact incremental/streaming features are impossible without lookahead re-encoding (21% rel. error for a 2 s prefix [measured-now]).

Audio conditioning is on MuseTalk's fixed 50 Hz / 25 fps timeline: 2 Whisper steps per model frame, window 10 steps x 5 hidden layers = [50,384]. Left padding must not scale with output fps (audio_processor.py:18-45).
Each turn is one whole-utterance upload; there is no streamed-audio API. TTS must finish the full WAV first, so the full TTS time sits in response latency.

All GPU work shares the legacy default CUDA stream (trt_runtime.py:538 uses current_stream). Whisper encodes in the prep thread serialize with UNet/VAE kernels, and the trailing .cpu() waits for any queued batch.

Per-turn setup (asyncio.to_thread ffmpeg, run_in_executor(None) PCM load) and aiortc's per-packet audio/video encode share the default asyncio executor. Kokoro also runs in-process via asyncio.to_thread.
Kokoro service holds a single RLock around init and synthesis, so at most one synthesis runs at a time (~8.8 audio-s/s at 16 threads).
CPU budget at 300 fps: 32 threads x 1000/300 = ~107 thread-ms per frame, but only 16 physical cores. Chin alignment, compose, libx264 (~2 ms/frame measured in live log) and WebRTC all draw on it.
VRAM: 12 GB total; the live server uses ~5 GB. A co-located GPU TTS must fit beside it (Kokoro inferred ~0.5-1 GB; OmniVoice ~6.4 GB [doc]).
Generation run-ahead per stream is bounded by WEBRTC_VIDEO_MAX_QUEUE_FRAMES=400 (20 s at 20 fps) and a 30 s push timeout in strict_fifo mode.
Exact-silence semantics (whole-file digital zero decoded before resampling) and the no-per-frame-quiet-gating rule are explicit product decisions in code and docs.
Product rule short_reply_seconds=3: replies under 3 s keep the idle body pose but still render the UNet mouth (motion_transitions.py:133).
Guardrail for this study: GPU not touched. All timings here are CPU-only, and another process held the GPU at 99% during measurement.

readers.summary: HISTORIAN REPORT. (a) Chronology: MuseTalk throughput work has gone through five eras. (1) Mar 2026, RTX 3090 HLS: lifecycle fixes, a single-thread shared GPU scheduler, the _memory_bucket=1 deadlock fix, a CPU compose rewrite (avg_compose 1.1 s->0.145 s, c8 cadence 5.2->2.3 s), PE precompute, torch.compile (-12% GPU batch), a finish-nearest-chunk policy and max_batch 48 all shipped. Worker counts, batch_size sweeps, persistent/in-process NVENC, GPU-resident conditioning/latents, vectorized prompts, SDPA and CPU thread caps were all closed with no change of tier [doc:archive_hls_throughput_experiment_history.md; current_model_backend_findings.md; CPU_OPTIMIZATION_ANALYSIS.md]. (2) Mar-Jul backend era: the monolithic TRT VAE was closed on a gray-face correctness failure (MAE 0.34). Stagewise TRT VAE and then ModelOpt ONNX/QDQ 5-stage VAE INT8 shipped (1.29x VAE, +11-18% WebRTC plateau). Whole-stage up_block_3 INT8 was rejected twice (mae 0.019, colour/texture). Static bs8 UNet TRT split8 shipped (UNet -35%; WebRTC +7-10% on 3090, +2-4% on RTX 6000 Ada), while the dynamic UNet TRT failed correctness. An exact bs16 UNet TRT (44.9 vs 51.8 ms split8) was validated on the 3090 in July but has never been built on this 4070S. The 224/192 ROI was rejected as too blurry. Compose ROI-shrink (3.12x) and the batched WebRTC callback shipped [doc:current_unet_trt_throughput_findings_2026-05-29.md; docs/musetalk_quantization_optimization_plan.md; docs/webrtc_generation_optimization_results_2026-07-03.md]. (3) 2026-09-22, this 4070S: compiled TAESD replaced the SD-VAE (VAE 138->6.83 ms @bs8; e2e 47.6->209-241 fps). Compile/late-crop on the SD-VAE were measured but superseded, and FP8 was flagged but never tried [doc:docs/musetalk_4070s_pipeline_component_analysis_2026-09-22.md]. (4) 2026-09-27: the TAESD + 100% chin offline harness measured 204.6/215 fps serial, 250.8 pipelined standard, and 184.9/193.4 with chin alignment. With the accepted refined seam it is 163-169 fps, and the diversity batch ran at 148-171 [doc:experiments/chin_fps_validation_20260927/README.md; chin_seam_refinement_20260927/PERFORMANCE_EXPLANATION.md]. (b) Gap: on every GPU, live WebRTC has run below model-path capacity. On the 3090 the observed/implied ratio was about 0.80-0.85 (55.9 vs 65.7; 62.5-65 vs ~78; 70.8-72 vs ~86 fps). On the RTX 6000 Ada the observed figure equalled batch/avg_gpu_batch (72.5-78 fps, later 108-114 fps), so the live plateau was the serial GPU turn itself. Strict smooth 20 fps capacity never exceeded 4 streams on any GPU [doc:current_cross_server_throughput_findings.md; load_test_webrtc_rtx6000ada_int8_trt_unet_split8_20fps_20260608.md]. The documented causes are: a synchronous one-thread GPU turn with a blocking D2H in vae.decode_latents [inferred-from-code: hls_gpu_scheduler.py:1471 -> vae.py:180]; bucket padding and fairness slicing; unwarmed-bucket live compiles and 30 s tail stalls; CPU compose and per-frame asyncio handoff (both fixed); HLS per-chunk encode and NVENC session limits; host oversubscription and the GIL (1,150 threads, 11 GB RSS at 8 streams); Whisper prep sharing the GPU; TRT VRAM residency OOMs; and strict FIFO with a 2 s prebuffer, which turns cadence deficits into stalls. Live multi-stream capacity with TAESD on this 4070S has never been measured. The only records are C1-C2 on 2026-09-15 (FP16 stagewise VAE + PyTorch UNet, 29.4 fps each) and a 3-peer smoke test on 2026-09-27 [doc:/workspace/benchmarks/baseline-comparison.md; experiments/chinese_bob_webrtc_20260927/README.md]. Arithmetic: 300 fps allows 3.33 ms of GPU per frame. Today's work is UNet 3.18 ms + TAESD 0.86 ms = about 4.0 ms/frame, a ~250 fps ceiling that matches the 250.8 fps offline measurement. Reaching 300 therefore needs three things: (1) remove at least 0.7 ms/frame from the UNet, which is about 78% of GPU time; (2) get live serialization loss close to zero; (3) spread about 5.5 ms/frame of chin CPU work across worker processes. On (3): FaceMesh+IPC is 3.0-3.3 ms/frame and mask/compose/warp 2.0-2.6 ms/frame; at 300 fps that is about 1.7 cores of CPU. Transferable SoulX lessons from this same card [doc:SoulX PRO_40FPS_ITERATION_LOG_2026-09-21.md; PRO_THROUGHPUT_PLAN_2026-09-21.md]: running two concurrent sessions on a saturated GPU added +1.3%. FP8 brings little: GEMM is capped at the 142 TFLOPS FP16-accumulate tier, and TRT 10.9 has no FP8 Conv3d kernel. CUDA graphs only paid off where host-issue-bound (+7.2%). The lever that worked was decoder block-bypass plus distillation (19.6->30.2 fps), whose failure mode was soft (lost detail); pruning the generator (DiT blocks) broke lip sync. (c/d) Quality gates: UNet TRT requires mae_max<=0.01 and max_abs<=0.5 on real scheduler captures. For the VAE, crop mae should be <=0.010, and anything near 0.019 is rejected. TAESD ROI mae of 0.011-0.016 is accepted. The chin checks require exact mask/pixel equality, zero change to protected lip pixels, and SHA-identical sequential vs pipelined output. SyncNet (models/syncnet/latentsync_syncnet.pt) is used only as an uncalibrated, crop-sensitive relative diagnostic. Visual A/B uses labelled same-speed videos with a mouth zoom. User decisions: the 224 ROI was rejected as too blurry; SD-VAE and TAESD were judged essentially the same; speed was preferred over the INT8/FP16 visual difference. TAESD with the native encoder, 100% chin alignment, the refined seam and the expressive H3 source is REQUIRED. Risky arms are allowed if gated on video with a one-line rollback, and every round ends with a labelled comparison video.

unet.summary:
I probed the MuseTalk v1.5 UNet on the RTX 4070 SUPER using real UNet I/O captures (/workspace/benchmarks/same-avatar/unet-captures) as inputs. FLOPs per frame are 177.8 GFLOP [measured-now]. The shipping TRT engine runs bs8 in 24.0-24.6 ms, which is 3.0-3.08 ms/frame and ~58-59 TFLOPS [measured-now]. Called back-to-back with nothing else running, the UNet alone tops out at 331 fps (341 fps with a CUDA graph) [measured-now]. For 300 fps the UNet has to get to about 2.35 ms/frame or less, because TAESD takes 0.86 ms/frame [doc]. So the UNet as it ships cannot support 300 fps.

What the engine spends its time on, by kernel [measured-now]: convolutions 36.6%, matrix multiplies (GEMMs) 27.2%, pointwise 22.3%, attention 5.3%, slice/reformat 4.9%, GroupNorm reductions 3.7%. About 31% of the time (7.4 ms per bs8 call) is spent outside the tensor cores. Much of that comes from the production converter splitting every GroupNorm into many small layers: 308 of the engine's 1798 layers, and 1250 kernels per call.

Every convolution and GEMM in the shipping engine already uses FP16 kernels with FP16 accumulation. On this card that is the same peak throughput as FP8, which is why FP8 cannot help here.

- **FP8 is a dead end on this card with TensorRT 10.3.** I built small TRT engines for single blocks, kept in memory only. With FP8 Q/DQ, TRT picks no FP8 convolution kernel: it keeps the FP16 convolution, fakes the quantization in extra pointwise kernels, and re-dequantizes the weights on every call. The result is 1.25x to 6.9x slower than FP16. FP8 GEMM kernels do get selected, but the transformer blocks still end up slower than FP16.
- **INT8 Q/DQ uses real INT8 convolution and GEMM kernels.** The ResNet blocks run 1.8-2.1x faster (122-195 TOPS). The 1024-token transformer block gains almost nothing (1.02x).
- **Whole-UNet estimates at bs8** (sum of 11 per-block engines built from ONNX kept in RAM):
  - Better FP16 build (ONNX-parser path): 20.58 ms, 14% faster than shipping.
  - INT8 on all convs and linears: 14.36 ms, 40% faster than shipping.
- **INT8 quality.** Naive INT8 gives 7.1% latent error and 41.8 dB PSNR against the FP16 decode. That is about 18x the shipping FP16 engine's error, and it would fail the repo's validation threshold (MAE 0.01).
- **Native bs16 FP16 engine** (built in memory with the production torch_tensorrt settings): 45.34 ms, 8.7% faster than two bs8 calls; 44.63 ms with a CUDA graph.
- **Two engine copies on two CUDA streams** (two execution contexts sharing one set of weights): 5% faster.
- **Host side.** The TRT call releases the Python GIL. But the thread issuing the calls keeps one CPU core 100% busy spin-waiting while the GPU works, about 24 ms of CPU per bs8 call.

Verdict for the UNet side: 300 fps is borderline reachable in FP16 only by stacking the better engine build, native bs16 and CUDA graphs (about 2.2-2.3 ms/frame, no headroom) [inferred]. It is comfortably reachable with mixed INT8 that passes a quality check (about 1.7-2.0 ms/frame, a ~360-380 fps GPU ceiling) [inferred]. 400 fps needs INT8 plus pruning or distillation of the UNet.

None of this covers the serving path (scheduler, encoding, WebRTC), which historically capped at ~112 fps [doc] and is not measured here.

conclusions: The shipping UNet cannot support 300 fps. It runs at 3.0-3.08 ms/frame [measured-now]; together with TAESD 0.86 ms/frame [doc] the GPU ceiling is about 250 fps, which matches the doc's 250.8. Even the UNet alone, back-to-back, tops out at 331 fps (341 fps with a CUDA graph) [measured-now].

FP8 is ruled out on this card with TensorRT 10.3. With FP8 Q/DQ, TRT keeps the FP16 convolution kernels, fakes the quantization in extra pointwise kernels and re-dequantizes the weights every call, so it ends up 1.25x to 6.9x slower than FP16 [measured-now]. FP8 GEMM kernels exist and are selected, but they do not beat the FP16-accumulate kernels TRT already uses; on consumer Ada cards FP8 with FP32 accumulation has the same peak as FP16 with FP16 accumulation [measured-now kernels; peak figures from NVIDIA's Ada spec]. torch._scaled_mm's 1.6-2.3x gain is only against PyTorch FP16, which accumulates in FP32 [measured-now].

INT8 is the only real low-precision option. It uses genuine INT8 kernels (sm80 xmma i8i32), gives 1.8-2.1x on ResNet and convolution blocks, 1.5x on 64-token transformers, and about nothing (1.02x) on 1024-token transformers [measured-now]. The whole-UNet INT8 estimate is 14.36 ms per bs8 (1.80 ms/frame), about 360+ fps with TAESD [measured-now sum of blocks; inferred fps].

Naive INT8 quality is not good enough yet: 7% latent error and 41.8 dB PSNR, about 18x the shipping FP16 engine's error [measured-now]. The up1 block is the most sensitive (21.7% error on its own output). Workable INT8 needs mixed precision (up1 and the 1024-token transformers kept FP16), calibration across many avatars, and possibly quantization-aware training or distillation, then a side-by-side video check of lip sync and jawline.

About 31% of the shipping engine's time is outside the tensor cores [measured-now]. Most of it traces to how the production converter (torch_tensorrt) splits every GroupNorm into many small layers. Building the same UNet through the ONNX parser is 14% faster at bs8 (20.58 vs 24.04 ms) [measured-now sum of blocks]. On single blocks the production converter is 1.09-1.53x slower than the ONNX path [measured-now].

Batching helps only a little. A native bs16 engine is 8.7% faster than two bs8 calls (45.34 vs 49.29 ms), 9.5% with a CUDA graph (44.63 ms) [measured-now]. The eager curve is nearly flat past bs16 (bs32 is only 4% better per frame) [measured-now]. Running two engine copies on two streams adds 5% [measured-now]. Batches larger than 16 are not worth pursuing.

The FP16-only route (ONNX-built engine, native bs16, CUDA graph) should land at about 2.2-2.3 ms/frame, which gives roughly 300-310 fps with TAESD and no headroom [inferred]. A robust 300 fps, or the 400 fps stretch, needs the mixed-INT8 UNet. 400 fps (UNet at 1.55 ms/frame or less) probably also needs pruning plus distillation of the UNet, the approach that worked for SoulX on this GPU [inferred].

Host side: the TRT call releases the Python GIL, but the thread issuing calls keeps one CPU core 100% busy spin-waiting while the GPU works (about 24 ms of CPU per bs8 call) [measured-now]. CUDA graphs cut the launch cost from 4.57 ms to 0.89 ms per call but do not remove the spin. Setting the CUDA device to blocking-sync mode, or using one dedicated GPU-feeding thread, would free that core for encoding and compositing [inferred].

Suggested UNet plan, in order: (0) free disk and host RAM; a full-UNet build needs about 11 GB of host RAM [measured-now] and each engine artifact is ~2.2 GB [measured-now], while the disk has 1.4 GB free; (1) CUDA-graph the UNet call; (2) build a native bs16 FP16 engine through the ONNX parser, or add a fused GroupNorm to the torch_tensorrt path; (3) mixed INT8 Q/DQ using the repo's existing modelopt ONNX Q/DQ tooling from the VAE INT8 work, block by block, starting with down1-3, mid, up0 and up2, checked against the latent-error threshold plus video; (4) two execution contexts sharing weights; (5) only if 400 fps is required, a pruned and distilled UNet. Drop FP8 and batches above 16.

None of these numbers include the serving path. Live WebRTC with TAESD has never been measured above 2-3 streams, and historically the serving path capped at about 112 fps [doc]. The ~1.6-2.2x UNet improvement discussed here only matters once the scheduler, encoding and WebRTC can push 300 fps.

taesd.summary:
I measured the TAESD decoder path on the RTX 4070 SUPER (56 SMs, 48 MB L2, 220 W cap), using real post-UNet latents from /workspace/benchmarks/same-avatar/unet-captures (128 frames) and the vendored models/taesd weights with the repo's convention (decode the scaled latent, then /2+0.5 and clamp). All numbers are [measured-now] unless marked otherwise.

- **Current decoder:** torch.compile max-autotune TAESD runs at 5.91 ms per batch of 8 (0.739 ms/frame). On this card that mode is really default compile plus CUDA graphs: inductor skips its autotuning on GPUs with fewer than 68 SMs, and forcing it gave no gain.
- **Row crop:** decoding only the latent rows the blend uses always changes some pixels until you decode everything (the receptive field is 18.1 latent rows, 145 px). A crop of the feature maps at the 64/128/256-resolution stage inputs, with the correct halo, is bit-exact (max_abs 0) and saves about 27%.
- **TensorRT FP16:** full decode is 0.486 ms/frame. With the exact crop and uint8 BGR NHWC output it is 0.345 ms/frame, 2.1x faster than live.
- **Second CUDA stream:** gives at most 2%. The TRT UNet already fills the GPU.
- **Whole GPU path:** the live-equivalent path (TRT UNet batch of 8 + compiled TAESD + post-process + pinned copy to CPU) measures 258.7 fps. Swapping in the cropped TRT TAESD gives 297.0 fps. Also turning on torch_tensorrt's CUDA-graph mode for the UNet gives 304.6 fps, with 3.28 ms/frame against the 3.33 ms budget.
- **What limits 300 fps:** after these changes the UNet is about 89% of GPU time (2.93 ms/frame even with graphs). The margin is about 1.5%, and it does not yet include Whisper/audio features, positional encoding, chin compose or serving.
- **Handoff and compose:** the GPU-to-CPU handoff is negligible (18 us/frame). The CPU resize-and-blend costs 0.35-0.47 ms/frame, versus about 5 us/frame if done on the GPU.

The live api_server (pid 3240171) was not running at any point: the GPU showed 0-4 MiB before every run and only my own PID. I deleted the inductor/Triton caches (up to 106 MB); the scratch directory is now about 240 KB and the GPU is back to 1 MiB.

Best decoder option: a TensorRT FP16 engine of the staged exact crop that outputs uint8 BGR NHWC directly (0.345 ms/frame, bit-exact crop, within 1 LSB). It saves about 0.39 ms/frame versus live and moves the whole GPU path from 258.7 to 297.0 fps [measured-now]. The engine is about 3 MB and builds in about 15 s, so it can be built at startup with nothing written to disk.

Crop at the feature-map level, never in latent space. A latent-space crop is never exact below a full decode (receptive field 145 px). The staged crop is exact at every halo it needs and is as fast as the lossy h=4 latent crop [measured-now].

The crop start row must be set per avatar from its mask. Standard avatars read from row 110-111. fixed_face_height (_fh1) avatars read from row 85, so a hard-coded crop at 104 would corrupt them. Use a few preset rows (for example R=80 and R=104; 0.403 vs 0.350 ms/frame) [measured-now].

Turning on torch_tensorrt.runtime.set_cudagraphs_mode(True) for the live UNet is a nearly free win. Output is bit-exact, GPU time drops 5%, and host time per call drops from 4.5 ms to under 0.3 ms with no blocking. Together with the cropped TRT TAESD it measures 304.6 fps on the GPU path [measured-now]. Before shipping, check whether outputs are overwritten by the next call.
A second CUDA stream for TAESD is not worth building. Overlap is 0.6-1.7%, and two UNets on two streams gain nothing, because one UNet already fills the power-capped GPU [measured-now].

300 fps is reachable on the GPU in isolation (304.6 fps measured) but with only about 1.5% margin. That excludes Whisper/audio features, positional encoding, compose and serving overhead. Reliable 300 fps, and certainly 400 fps (2.5 ms/frame, below the 2.93 ms/frame UNet alone), needs a faster UNet: INT8/FP8, a native bs16 engine, pruning or distillation [inferred-from-measurements].

INT8 TensorRT TAESD would save about 0.2 ms/frame more (0.147 ms/frame, taking the ceiling to about 320 fps, inferred and not measured end-to-end). PSNR is 46.3 dB but the worst pixel is off by 0.18, so it needs a visual check first [measured-now].

Moving the handoff and compose to the GPU is optional for throughput. The current handoff costs 18 us/frame. CPU compose costs 0.35-0.47 ms/frame, about 0.1-0.14 of a core at 300 fps, versus about 5 us/frame on the GPU. Its real value is less Python work under the GIL and a shorter critical path; it also fits a later on-GPU encode step [measured-now].

Hazards for any multi-threaded or multi-stream serving design [measured-now]: (a) the default torch_tensorrt runtime blocks the calling thread for a whole UNet call, and host time per call grew from 4.5 to 14 ms when another Python thread was busy. (b) TAESD compiled with max-autotune/CUDA graphs crashed when called from a second thread (AssertionError in cudagraph_trees). (c) inductor max-autotune does no autotuning on this 56-SM card. (d) the decoder must run with cudnn.benchmark=True (11% difference).

cpu.summary: CPU/encoder probe on a Ryzen 9 7950X + RTX 4070 SUPER, run CPU-only with the GPU idle. The live api_server (pid 3240171) was not running during any run. Main result: the 7950X has enough CPU for 300 fps and for 400 fps. A combined, paced load test ran 15 and 20 streams at 20 fps each. Each stream did the real compose_frame, a stand-in for chin-aligned compose, the current PyAV colour conversion, native VP8 encode at 2.5 Mbps, RTP+SRTP+UDP send and Opus audio, with one real refined-FaceMesh tracker process per stream alongside. It needed 10.6 logical CPUs at 300 fps and 12.5-13.1 at 400 fps, out of 32 [measured-now]. The real limit is the single Python process. The per-frame CPU chain saturates at about 6 cores per process because of the GIL: about 570-665 fps with the chin path and 820-990 fps standard [measured-now]. With all 20 streams in one process, per-frame work averaged 48 ms, about the whole 50 ms frame period, and 19 frames were late. Split into 4 processes of 5 streams, the same load ran at 12.6-23.8 ms with 0 late frames. Three more findings. First, the live H.264 path actually encodes with libx264 at the medium preset, not NVENC: the NVENC patch in api_server has no effect on aiortc 1.14. That costs about 26 ms of CPU per frame (7.9 cores at 300 fps, 10.8 at 400 fps). Second, NVENC on this GeForce card stops at 12 concurrent sessions and uses about 200 MB of VRAM each. Third, PyAV's bgr24-to-yuv420p conversion costs 1.5 ms per frame at 512 width, and cv2 does the same conversion in 0.21 ms with at most 1 LSB difference. Whisper-tiny for 8 s of audio takes 14 ms warm on the GPU, far below the doc's 0.88 s.

conclusions: CPU fits. At 300 fps (15 streams) with 100% chin alignment and native VP8 on 1 codec thread, the measured load is 10.6 of 32 logical CPUs (33%). At 400 fps (20 streams) it is 12.5-13.1 (39-41%) [measured-now]. Adding an estimated 1.5-3.5 CPUs for GPU-feeding threads (CUDA spin-wait) and the rest of the aiortc stack [inferred] gives about 12-14 CPUs at 300 fps (roughly 56-62% headroom) and 14-16.6 at 400 fps (roughly 48-56% headroom). Budget view: at 300 fps the box offers 106.7 CPU-ms per frame and the chin path uses about 35. At 400 fps it offers 80 and uses about 31-33. CPU is not what limits reaching 300 fps; the GPU is (UNet alone at about 3.1 ms/frame caps near 320 fps).

The real CPU-side limit is the Python GIL in a single process. The full per-frame chain tops out at about 570-665 fps per process with the chin path, and 820-990 fps standard, at about 6 cores. At 400 fps with chin in one process, per-frame work averaged 48 ms against a 50 ms frame period, with 19 late frames. Split across 4 processes of 5 streams: 12.6-23.8 ms and 0 late [measured-now]. The live server would also run its GPU scheduler thread and asyncio loop under the same GIL, which fits the historical live plateau of about 112 fps. The plan needs one GPU process plus 3-4 or more media-worker processes (compose, chin, colour conversion, encode, RTP, audio) connected by shared memory. Decoded faces are about 196 KB each, so 400 fps is only about 79 MB/s.

Bug: api_server's NVENC patch has no effect on aiortc 1.14. `h264.create_encoder_context` does not exist; `H264Encoder._encode_frame` hardcodes `av.CodecContext.create("libx264", "w")` [inferred-from-code]. The live log confirms codec=libx264 [doc:experiments/chinese_bob_webrtc_20260927/wall_api.log]. That path costs about 26 ms of CPU per frame at concurrency: 7.85 cores at 300 fps and 10.8 at 400 fps [measured-now]. Replace it with native VP8 on 1 thread (1.85 / 2.79 cores), libx264 ultrafast on 1 thread (0.69 / 1.07 cores), or NVENC.

NVENC alone cannot serve 15-20 streams. The driver caps it at 12 concurrent sessions, and each takes about 200 MB of VRAM (2.47 GB for 12), which competes with larger TensorRT UNet engines. Encoder throughput is not the issue: about 2600 fps at 100% utilisation. Options are a hybrid (up to 12 NVENC sessions, CPU VP8 or x264 for the rest) or all-CPU native VP8 at 1 thread, which is cheap enough (2.8 cores at 400 fps).

Set libvpx to 1 thread per stream. aiortc's default of 2 threads at 512x832 costs 35-45% more CPU per frame under concurrency (8.4 vs 6.2 ms at 15 streams, 10.0 vs 7.0 at 20) with no gain in aggregate throughput.

Replace `av.VideoFrame.from_ndarray(bgr, 'bgr24').reformat('yuv420p')` with `cv2.cvtColor(bgr, cv2.COLOR_BGR2YUV_I420)` followed by `from_ndarray(..., 'yuv420p')`. It drops from 1.51-1.56 ms to 0.21 ms per frame, with the same limited range and at most 1 LSB difference. PyAV has a width-512 slow path (from_ndarray 0.97 ms vs 0.06-0.13 ms at other widths). The change also roughly doubles the in-process compose-plus-conversion GIL ceiling (2400 to 4480 fps).

FaceMesh is the largest CPU cost on the chin path: 2.8-4.0 cores at 300 fps and 4.8-5.8 at 400 fps under burst-aligned pacing [measured-now]. It fits, but tracking mode needs one stateful tracker per stream. Face-crop size barely changes the cost (256x256: 2.68 ms CPU; full frame: 3.43 ms). The machine saturates at about 1900 fps of FaceMesh, about 5x the 400 fps target.

Whisper-tiny should stay on the GPU. Warm, 8 s of audio costs 14 ms in total, of which about 3 ms is GPU time (about 0.02 ms of GPU per frame). On CPU it costs 70 ms (8 threads) to 350 ms (1 thread). The doc's 0.88 s was not reproduced warm or cold (cold is about 150 ms). Because the encoder always runs a padded 30 s window, batch short streaming TTS chunks across streams.

Colour conversion, compose, RTP and SRTP, and Opus together use under 1.5 cores at 400 fps. With the current PyAV conversion they are still GIL-heavy. The 384x672 frame size lowers encode cost (VP8 4.5 ms per frame at 20 streams) but is not needed for CPU fit.
